principles.text: Ship many small products. Only about 5% of his 35 startups worked, so launch volume is what produces a winner.
Every startup has a 24-hour version: a headline, a buy button and one feature.
Sell it before you build it. Only payment validates an idea; a waitlist isn't enough.
No free plan as a solopreneur. Start with one-time payments and build painkillers, not vitamins.
Market by building: launch free, single-feature mini-apps that promote your main startup.

sampleQA.question: I have a product, no audience and no budget. How do I get the first users?

answer.text: Launch on platforms that don't care about follower count: Hacker News, Reddit, Product Hunt, Uneed, TinyLaunch. Then share the results on X and use that audience for the next launch.
Spend at least an hour on the headline. He calls it 80% of a successful launch.
Still no visitors? Turn one feature into a free, no-signup tool and use it as a funnel to the paid product.
If the launch flops, don't add features. Rebrand or reposition with a different headline and relaunch everywhere.

sampleQA.question: Should I offer a free plan or a subscription?

answer.text: Skip the free plan when you're solo. Only about 3% of free users upgrade, so you'd need 10,000 users to make $3,000 at $10/month.
Start with one-time payments. Add a subscription only when there's demand or the product delivers recurring value.
Offer two plans so the cheaper one acts as a price anchor for the higher one.

sampleQA.question: How long should I work on one idea before moving on?

answer.text: Drop ideas that take longer than a month to build. A 6-month estimate usually turns into 12 and leads to burnout.
Judge fit from launch traffic. After about 1,000 visitors he knows whether a product could work.
Don't force a startup with no initial traction. Launch several, see what sticks, then focus.
Once something has traction, stay with it. DataFast took 512 days of shipping to reach $20K MRR.
